item.mechanism: Stress-induced reorientation (position switching) of interstitial atoms (O or N) in a bcc lattice causes mechanical energy loss (Snoek relaxation).
item.operating_conditions: Forced vibration at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz; temperature range 300–1100 K; maximum strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; heating rate 2 K min⁻¹
item.supporting_observation: Thermally activated relaxation peaks where peak temperature increases and peak height decreases with increasing frequency; activation energies of 2.06, 2.40, and 4.06 eV for base, O-2, and N-2 HEAs respectively.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is amplitude-independent, unlike other damping mechanisms (e.g., dislocation motion) which are amplitude-dependent; the peaks are broader than Debye peaks due to the variety of local atomic configurations.
item.alternatives_considered: Irreversible rearrangement of crystal defects (dislocations, phase boundaries) which deteriorate over time and at high temperatures; magnetic domain boundaries.
quotes: the mechanical energy loss originates from the stress-induced ordering of interstitials
the stress-induced position switch of interstitial atoms gives rise to the corresponding internal friction peaks
the Snoek-type relaxation is intrinsically amplitude-independent

item.mechanism: Ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs or ONCs) form due to preferential occupation of interstitial sites adjacent to light atoms (Zr, Ti), contributing to specific low-temperature damping peaks and enhancing ductility via strain hardening.
item.operating_conditions: As-cast state; room temperature tensile testing; internal friction measurements showing low-temperature peaks at 577 K (O-2) and corresponding nitrogen peaks.
item.supporting_observation: STEM-ABF images show oxygen occupying interstitial sites adjacent to Zr/Ti; Atom Probe Tomography reveals O-rich clusters; a distinct low-temperature damping peak appears in doped alloys but not the base alloy.
item.scope_limits: Ordered complexes form only when interstitial concentration is sufficient (e.g., 2.0 at%); in the base HEA, trace oxygen (0.377 at%) is randomly distributed without forming ordered complexes.
item.alternatives_considered: Randomly distributed interstitial atoms which contribute to high-temperature damping peaks but do not form the specific low-temperature peaks associated with ordered complexes.
quotes: oxygen tends to prefer interstitial positions adjacent to lattice sites, which are occupied by light atoms (i.e., Zr and/or Ti), accumulating to the so-called ordered oxygen complexes
The formation of ordered oxygen complexes gives rise to the additional low-temperature peak
ordered interstitial complexes–mediated strain hardening contributes to the improved mechanical performance

item.mechanism: High configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion in HEAs impede atomic position switches of interstitials, raising the activation energy and peak temperature for Snoek relaxation compared to conventional alloys.
item.system: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi-based HEAs compared to conventional bcc interstitial alloys
item.operating_conditions: High-temperature damping applications (peak temperatures ~730–800 K); comparison with traditional alloys at lower temperatures.
item.supporting_observation: Peak temperatures of current HEAs (737, 747, 730 K) are ~100 K higher than traditional alloys; activation energies (2.06–4.06 eV) are significantly higher than those in conventional Snoek-type alloys.
item.scope_limits: This effect relies on the specific combination of high configurational entropy and large lattice distortion found in these refractory HEAs; not stated if it applies to non-refractory or low-entropy alloys.
item.alternatives_considered: Conventional alloys where lattice distortion is lower, leading to lower activation barriers and lower peak temperatures.
quotes: This effect gives rise to the high activation temperatures and barrier energies for the interstitial reorientation steps and the resulting high-temperature damping capability
Both, T p and H of the current HEAs are much higher than those of interstitially doped conventional alloys

item.mechanism: Randomly distributed interstitial atoms (RDIAs) provide the primary contribution to the high-temperature damping capacity, with peak height scaling linearly with solute concentration.
item.operating_conditions: Internal friction measurements at 1.0 Hz; decomposition of relaxation spectra into high-temperature peaks.
item.supporting_observation: In N-2 HEA, ~94.7% of nitrogen is randomly distributed, resulting in the strongest damping peak (tanδ max ~0.027); peak height correlates with the concentration of randomly distributed atoms.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism dominates when ordered complex formation is low; in O-2 HEA, a significant portion (18.5%) forms ordered complexes, reducing the relative contribution of random atoms compared to N-2.
item.alternatives_considered: Ordered interstitial complexes which contribute to ductility and low-temperature peaks but are less effective for maximizing the total high-temperature damping peak height.
quotes: randomly distributed interstitial atoms improve mechanical damping
For a specific alloy system, the magnitude of the Snoek damping peak height follows a linear relationship with the solute element concentration
As most of the nitrogen is interstitially randomly distributed, the N-2 HEA shows the strongest damping peak among all three HEAs studied here

item.mechanism: Interstitial solid-solution strengthening increases yield strength, with nitrogen providing stronger strengthening than oxygen due to its larger atomic size.
item.system: O-2 and N-2 HEAs compared to base HEA
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
item.supporting_observation: Yield strength increased from ~810 MPa (base) to 1138 MPa (O-2) and 1362 MPa (N-2); N-2 HEA is ~224 MPa stronger than O-2 HEA.
item.scope_limits: The strengthening effect is observed in the as-cast state; the text notes that interstitial reinforcement by nitrogen is more effective than oxygen.
item.alternatives_considered: Traditional high-damping alloys where high damping and high strength are mutually exclusive; this mechanism allows simultaneous enhancement.
quotes: The interstitial doped HEAs have a strong solid-solution strengthening, i.e., the yield strength was increased to 1138 and 1362 MPa for the O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively
Interstitial reinforcement by nitrogen is more effective than that conveyed by oxygen doping
With the addition of 2.0 at % nitrogen, the larger atomic size of nitrogen (atomic radius of 0.75 Å) compared to that of oxygen (0.65 Å) leads to higher strengthening

item.mechanism: The variety of local atomic configurations in complex solid-solution alloys leads to a broad distribution of thermally activated site-switching events, resulting in asymmetrically broadened Snoek peaks.
item.operating_conditions: Internal friction measurements showing peak shapes at various frequencies.
item.supporting_observation: Relaxation peaks are much broader than a Debye peak and asymmetrically broadened; peak deconvolution reveals multiple overlapping processes.
item.scope_limits: This broadening is specific to compositionally complex solid-solution alloys; it complicates peak deconvolution analysis compared to simple binary systems.
item.alternatives_considered: A single relaxation process (Debye peak) which would occur in a simple lattice with uniform environments.
quotes: This effect leads to a Snoek signal in the current HEAs where the relaxation peaks are much broader than a Debye peak
This is a feature associated with the variety of interstitial relaxation processes involved in these massive solid solutions
Because of the complexity in alloy composition and the resulting multitude in local chemical environments in which the interstitial atoms switch their positions

item.mechanism: Ordered interstitial complexes (OICs) impede dislocation motion and provide strain hardening, thereby enhancing ductility without sacrificing strength.
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature tensile testing; ductility measured as elongation.
item.supporting_observation: Ductility of O-2 HEA doubled to ~20% compared to base HEA (~10.8%); attributed to ~18.5% of oxygen atoms forming ordered complexes.
item.scope_limits: In N-2 HEA, only ~5.3% of nitrogen forms ordered complexes, resulting in lower ductility (~11.9%) compared to O-2, though still better than base.
item.alternatives_considered: Mobile defects which cause damping but reduce strength; immobile defects which increase strength but reduce damping.
quotes: the ductility of the O-2 HEA was unexpectedly doubled, which has been earlier associated with the formation of ordered interstitial complexes that provide high strain hardening
ordered interstitial complexes contribute to the enhancement of ductility
the appearance of ordered nitrogen complexes that impede dislocation motion

item.mechanism: The high-temperature stability of the damping capacity is maintained because the relaxation process is reversible and not dependent on the rearrangement of structural defects.
item.operating_conditions: Long-term exposure to vibrations and elevated temperatures (up to ~800 K).
item.supporting_observation: Snoek relaxation is described as maintaining damping over long-term exposure, unlike traditional alloys where defects rearrange and aggregate, causing irreversible deterioration.
item.scope_limits: This stability is contrasted with traditional alloys where irreversible relaxation processes accelerate when service temperature increases.
item.alternatives_considered: Irreversible relaxation processes in traditional alloys involving dislocations, phase boundaries, or twin boundaries which deteriorate damping capacity over time.
quotes: both crystal defects and interfaces in these conventional alloys tend to rearrange and aggregate. As a result, the whole relaxation process is irreversible
the high damping capacity of the alloy class discussed here is amplitude independent and originates instead from the high configurational variety of the underlying interstitial relaxation processes
